questions.q: What's the real difference between an incident-response plan and a runbook?
options: There is no difference -- the terms are interchangeable
A plan covers policy-level decisions (who's notified, legal deadlines); a runbook is the tactical, step-by-step sequence a responder actually follows
A runbook only applies to compliance, not operations
A plan is written during an incident; a runbook is written beforehand
questions.explain: The plan answers who gets called and when; the runbook answers what a responder actually does, step by step, with an alert in front of them.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the six runbook phases?
options: Contain, Triage, Scope, Recover, Eradicate, After-action
Triage, Scope, Contain, Eradicate, Recover, After-action
After-action, Triage, Scope, Contain, Eradicate, Recover
Scope, Triage, Eradicate, Contain, Recover, After-action
questions.explain: The runbook walks a responder through Triage, Scope, Contain, Eradicate, Recover, and After-action, in that order.

questions.q: What does the Contain phase emphasize?
options: Shutting down the entire network as a precaution
Stopping the incident from getting worse without destroying evidence -- disabling the specific account or isolating the specific host, not the whole system
Immediately notifying the press
Deleting all logs related to the incident
questions.explain: Containment targets the specific account, address, or host involved, rather than taking a broader system offline unnecessarily.

questions.q: Why does the runbook define severity tiers (SEV1-SEV4) before any real incident happens?
options: Severity tiers are only cosmetic and don't affect response
So a responder under pressure matches an alert against an existing scale instead of inventing a severity judgment from scratch at 3 a.m.
Because Sentinel requires severity tiers to be defined before any rule can run
Severity tiers are decided case-by-case and never written down in advance
questions.explain: Deciding severity criteria calmly, in advance, means a stressed responder doesn't have to improvise a judgment call during a real incident.

questions.q: Why is writing the runbook now, with no real incident underway, deliberate rather than incidental?
options: It isn't deliberate -- it's just the next item on a checklist
A runbook drafted mid-incident is really just improvisation with better formatting; writing it calmly now gives the next real alert somewhere concrete to go
Runbooks can only legally be written outside of business hours
Hartwell is required by contract to write it this week
questions.explain: Writing it calmly, with both Owen's and Renee's input already folded in, means the next real alert from the new correlation rule has a real procedure to follow.
